newsitem.title: FRANCE: Suspected Algerian rebels cut throats of 12 - papers.
newsitem.headline: Suspected Algerian rebels cut throats of 12 - papers.

text.p: Suspected Moslem guerrillas have killed 12 people, including five members of one family, in the past few days, Algerian newspapers reported on Monday.
The five, including twin sisters aged 22, died when suspected rebels cut their throats in an attack on Friday night, al Khabar said.
The rebels broke into the family home in Laghouat, 340 km (210 miles) south of Algiers, the newspaper said, adding that they also cut the throat of the family dog.
Guerrillas shot and wounded the deputy mayor of Sidi Bouzid town and two other people on Sunday, al Khabar said. Sidi Bouzid lies 140 km (85 miles) from Laghouat.
On Friday night, attackers also cut the throats of five people in Tablat, 35 km (20 miles) south of Algiers, Liberte said.
The bodies of two other people, their throats cut, were found in Souaghi village, in Medea province, 70 km (45 miles) south of Algiers, Liberte said without giving more details.
In the town of Medea, a Moslem guerrilla stronghold, a bomb exploded on Saturday but caused no injuries, Liberte reported.
Security forces killed five guerrillas last week near Guerara village, 420 km (260 miles) south of Algiers, the paper said.

The five belonged to the Belmokhtar Group, which was suspected of killing 34 people, including 20 bus passengers, early in October at a fake roadblock in the nearby small town of Bouterkfine, Liberte added.

Separately, a Moslem militant leader Ahmed Zaoui was quoted on Monday by the London-based newspaper al Hayat as saying that Algeria's upcoming parliamentary elections would only prompt a worsening of the country's five-year-old strife.

"The whole issue is a play in which army generals and politicians trade parts to buy more time and impose a situation which will be difficult to overcome, and it is sure that the dangers will intensify rather than ebb," said Zaoui.
Zaoui, a leader of the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS), is under house arrest in Belgium.
About 60,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which the FIS had taken a commanding lead.
The government plans to hold multiparty parliamentary elections in May or June but bars the FIS from fielding candidates.
